# Positive-mass midpoint comparability and parity direction strata

Historical claim of scope (pending review here): proved quantitative geometric invariant. This result applies
even when all unnormalized coarse fiber volumes vanish and the positive
coarse projection is hollow. It does not assert that auxiliary affine
normalizations preserve a fine lattice or provide an OC mass allocation.
The missing-mass examples and the hollow-projection lemma are in
`candidate e306d42187c98e53`.

## 1. Bounded Minkowski volume gives two-sided shape control

Let m>=1. Fix a>0 and D>0, and let K,L be convex bodies in R^m such
that

    |L|>=a |K|,    |K+L|<=D |K|.                         (1)

Put kappa_j=vol_j(B_2^j), kappa_0=1, and define

    R=m(m+2),
    H=D kappa_m R^m / kappa_(m-1),
    rho=a kappa_m / [(m+1)2^m H^(m-1)],
    c=rho/R.                                            (2)

There are points p in K and q in L such that

    c(K-p) subset L-q subset H(K-p).                     (3)

Consequently the difference bodies and EVERY directional width obey

    c(K-K) subset L-L subset H(K-K),
    c width_K(u)<=width_L(u)<=H width_K(u)  for all u.     (4)

All constants depend only on m,a,D, not on eccentricities, relative
orientation, or the total volume scale. No near-equality hypothesis
in Brunn--Minkowski is used.

Proof. Apply the maximum-inscribed-simplex normalization to K, with
linear part T and center p, obtaining

    B_2^m subset K'=T(K-p) subset R B_2^m.

The elementary construction and the value R are proved in Section 1
of `candidate 7cb4b1bb7928127e`.
Apply the SAME affine map to L, writing L'=T(L-p). The hypotheses give

    |L'|>=a kappa_m,
    |K'+L'|<=D |K'|<=D kappa_m R^m.                      (5)

Translations in the sum do not affect its volume. If [b_0,b_1] is a
longest segment of L', then B_2^m+[b_0,b_1] is contained in K'+L'.
Its volume is kappa_m+kappa_(m-1)|b_1-b_0|, by slicing along the
segment. Hence diam(L')<=H.

For completeness, volume and diameter now give a quantitative inner
ball without assuming a smooth boundary. Let Delta be a maximum-volume
inscribed simplex of L'. Replacing each vertex by any point of L'
shows that the simplex-normalized L' is contained in [-1,1]^m. Thus

    |Delta| >= |L'|/(2^m m!) >= a kappa_m/(2^m m!).        (6)

Every facet of Delta has (m-1)-volume at most H^(m-1)/(m-1)!, by
Hadamard applied to its edge vectors. Therefore every altitude is at
least a kappa_m/(2^m H^(m-1)). The simplex centroid q' has distance
at least rho from every facet. It follows that

    rho B_2^m subset L'-q' subset H B_2^m.                (7)

The upper inclusion uses q' in L' and diam(L')<=H. For m=1 the same
calculation uses zero-dimensional facet volume one and remains valid.
Combining (7) with B_2^m subset K' subset R B_2^m gives

    (rho/R)K' subset L'-q' subset H K'.

Pull back by T, setting q=p+T^(-1)q', to obtain (3). Subtraction gives
the difference-body inclusions and their support-function form (4).

## 2. Hausdorff limits have the same direction space

Suppose K_l,L_l are contained in a common bounded region, converge in
Hausdorff distance to nonempty compact convex sets K_*,L_*, and obey
(1) with the SAME m,a,D. Then

    span(K_*-K_*)=span(L_*-L_*).                          (8)

In particular their affine dimensions are equal and their affine hulls
are parallel, even if the common dimension is zero or less than m.

Indeed support functions and directional widths converge uniformly
under Hausdorff convergence. Passing to the limit in (4) says that
K_* has width zero in a direction exactly when L_* does. The linear
span of a difference body is the orthogonal complement of its
zero-width directions, proving (8). Alternatively choose convergent
subsequences of the centers p_l in K_l and q_l in L_l and pass directly
to (3).

The conclusion is stronger than equality of ranks: the fixed constants
in (4) compare every directional thickness BEFORE the limit. It is
not a claim that K_* and L_* are translates or homothetic bodies.

## 3. Application to positive relative-mass coarse fibers

Let P be a fixed finite set of integer bases in Z^k. Suppose for each l
that Q_(l,z), z in P, are compatible compact convex fibers in R^m,
with total full coarse volume

    M_l=sum_(z in P)|Q_(l,z)|>0.

Nonempty zero-volume fibers may occur; the selected fibers below have
positive m-volume. Suppose all fibers have Hausdorff limits, and after
taking a subsequence their normalized masses have limits

    |Q_(l,z)|/M_l -> p_z.

Write P_+={z:p_z>0}. If z,w in P_+ have the same parity, their integer
midpoint j=(z+w)/2 is an actual compatible base. For all sufficiently
large l choose a fixed eta>0 with

    |Q_(l,z)|>=eta M_l,   |Q_(l,w)|>=eta M_l.

Compatibility and the inclusion of the midpoint fiber in the total
mass give

    |Q_(l,z)+Q_(l,w)| <= 2^m |Q_(l,j)| <= 2^m M_l
                         <=(2^m/eta)|Q_(l,z)|,
    |Q_(l,w)|>=eta |Q_(l,z)|.                            (9)

Thus Section 1 applies with a=eta and D=2^m/eta. It follows that ALL
positive limiting-weight fibers in a given parity class have the
same limiting direction space and affine dimension. There are at
most 2^k such direction strata, one per nonempty parity class; distinct
classes may have the same direction space.

The midpoint base must be included even if it was not initially named
among the selected positive sources. It has positive relative mass by
Brunn--Minkowski, so cannot be dropped as a zero-weight intermediate.
The statement assumes P contains every nonempty integer fiber, or
equivalently that the stated compatibility includes these intermediate
integer bases and their volumes are counted in M_l.

More generally P_+ itself is lattice-convex. If an integer j is a convex
combination sum t_i z_i of bases z_i in P_+, compatibility and
Brunn--Minkowski imply

    p_j >= (sum_i t_i p_(z_i)^(1/m))^m >0.               (10)

This uses only positive weights in the representation; zero weights
can be removed. Original compatibility first ensures that j is a
nonempty base in P. Hence P_+=conv(P_+) intersect Z^k.

Neither (9) nor (10) requires M_l to stay away from zero. They apply
to the hollow positive-support regime left open by a positive-volume
coarse limit. The statement also does not use the archived
nonhollow-projection normalization as an unstated hypothesis.

### 3.1. A stronger integer barycentric incidence rule

Suppose an integer base j has a fixed representation as a convex
combination of actual bases, and that a particular source z in P_+
occurs with coefficient lambda>0. Compatibility gives, for a suitable
translation t_l,

    lambda Q_(l,z)+t_l subset Q_(l,j).                   (11)

Choose one point in each of the other nonempty fibers to obtain this
translation. Hence the target's normalized mass has positive lower
limit, at least lambda^m p_z. Moreover, writing K=Q_(l,z), L=Q_(l,j),

    K+L subset lambda^(-1)(L-t_l)+L
        =(1+lambda^(-1))L-lambda^(-1)t_l.

The equality uses convexity of L. If |K|>=eta M_l, the two estimates
needed for Section 1 are therefore

    |L|>=lambda^m|K|,
    |K+L|<=(1+lambda^(-1))^m M_l
           <=[(1+lambda^(-1))^m/eta]|K|.                 (12)

The source and target have uniformly comparable directional widths and
the SAME limiting direction space. Every positive-relative-mass source
in the representation consequently shares the target's direction.
Sources of zero limiting weight need not have equal direction spaces;
their translated, scaled limiting fibers are only forced to lie inside
the target by (11).

Thus parity is one sufficient way to obtain integer barycentric
incidence, not the only one. This strengthened rule still allows the
different-direction examples: their surviving bases admit no integer
barycentric representation mixing those directions with positive
coefficients, apart from the trivial one-point representations.

## 4. Exact calibration: crossing directions force midpoint domination

In coarse rank one and continuous dimension two, put at bases -1,+1

    K_epsilon=[-1,1] times [-epsilon,epsilon],
    L_epsilon=[-epsilon,epsilon] times [-1,1],

and take their convex hull. Its actual middle integer fiber is

    Q_0=(K_epsilon+L_epsilon)/2
       =[-(1+epsilon)/2,(1+epsilon)/2]^2.

The three fiber areas are

    4epsilon, (1+epsilon)^2, 4epsilon,
    M_epsilon=1+10epsilon+epsilon^2.                      (13)

The endpoint segments have different limiting directions but the same
parity. Their normalized masses both tend to zero, while the midpoint
mass tends to one. This is exactly the behavior (9) requires; it is
not a counterexample to positive-weight comparability.

By contrast, the two different directions in Sections 1--2 of
`candidate e306d42187c98e53` occur
at adjacent bases of different parity. The three square directions in
that note's rank-two example occur at (1,0),(0,1),(1,1), also in three
different parity classes. Both examples satisfy the new constraint.

## 5. Scope for a compactness argument

The proved invariant is a uniform comparison of directional widths
inside each positive-mass parity class, and hence a restriction on
which lower-dimensional limit fibers can coexist with nonzero weight.
The class centers need not coincide, different classes need not have
parallel directions, and the probability laws on the limits need not
be intrinsic uniform measures. No cancellation of integer tilts or
sharp cap budget is inferred from the number of strata.

The normalizations used in Section 1 are auxiliary changes of variables
for a TWO-BODY geometric inequality. They may mix fine integer and
continuous coordinates. The proof does not apply them to the original
mixed problem, assume that its fine lattice remains dense, or assert
that independently chosen density lifts retain compatibility.
